overview.intro: The Gupta Age (c. 319-550 CE) is celebrated as the 'Golden Age' of ancient India for its political unification, administrative order and unrivalled achievements in education, science and culture. This chapter studies its two key sources - the Chinese pilgrim Fa-hien's account and the Allahabad Pillar Inscription of Harishena - the kings in chronological order, the Gupta administration, and contributions to education (Nalanda), science (Aryabhatta, Sushrutha's medical tradition) and culture (Kalidasa, Deogarh temple).

blocks.text: After the Mauryas, north India fragmented; the Kushanas and Satavahanas held parts of it until the Guptas rose from Magadha. Sri Gupta founded the line; Chandragupta I (r. 319-335 CE) married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi, issued the Gupta era, and took the title Maharajadhiraja. His son Samudragupta (r. 335-375) swept across India (except, notably, the far south's Keralaputra etc. and the Shakas left untouched) in the campaigns eulogised by his court poet Harishena on the Allahabad Pillar. Chandragupta II 'Vikramaditya' (r. 375-413/415) broke the Shaka power of Ujjain, married his daughter Prabhavati Gupta into the Vakataka house, and hosted the 'nine gems' including Kalidasa; Fa-hien visited during his reign. Skandagupta later repulsed the Huns; after him, weak successors and Hun pressure ended the empire by c. 550 CE.

Sources - Fa-hien's account. Fa-hien, a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim, travelled India 399-414 CE seeking true Buddhist texts. His Record of Buddhist Kingdoms describes the prosperous Ganga plains under Chandragupta II: people happy and honest; crimes rarely punished by mutilation (fines for most offences); vegetarianism common; Pataliputra's palace and charity houses; free hospitals (his remark about charitable institutions for the poor is famous). As a foreigner's eye-witness account, it balances court inscriptions with ordinary life and administration.

Sources - Allahabad Pillar Inscription. The Prayaga Prashasti, composed in Sanskrit (Champu style) by Harishena, is engraved on an Ashokan pillar at Allahabad (Prayagraj). It praises Samudragupta in detail: his conquests (Aryavarta campaigns against nine kings, Dakshinapatha campaigns of twelve, 'grihita'... etc.), his performance of ashvamedha, his talents as musician and poet. It is the main political source for the reign and a masterpiece of Gupta Sanskrit; historians cross-check its eulogy with coins and other records.

Kings in chronological order. Sri Gupta (founder, title Maharaja), Ghatotkacha, Chandragupta I (319-335 CE; Gupta era; Lichchhavi marriage), Samudragupta (335-375; 'Indian Napoleon', digvijaya; ashvamedha; veena-player on coins), Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (375-413/15; end of Shaka rule; Navaratnas; Fa-hien's host), Kumaragupta I (415-455; Nalanda's monastic founding per tradition; Worship of Kartikeya), Skandagupta (455-467; repulsed the Huns; Junagadh inscription - Sudarshana lake repaired), then weaker successors (Purugupta, Kumaragupta II, Budhagupta, Narasimhagupta 'Baladitya', Vishnugupta...) until c. 550 CE.

Administration. The king was supreme, aided by ministers (mantrins) and a hierarchy: the kumaramatyas (high officials), sandhi-vigrahika (war & peace), mahabaladhikrita (commander), dandapashika (justice/police). The empire split into bhukti (province, under uparika), vishaya (district, under vishayapati), and villages (gramika) - the bhukti-vishaya-grama ladder, recorded in land-grant charters. Land revenue from the peasant (1/4th to 1/6th of produce - bali/bhaga) fed the state; land grants (agrahara) to priests and temples spread agriculture and learning but later weakened central power. Standing army with war-office, cavalry, elephants; ports and roads kept trade flowing; gold dinars of Samudragupta/Chandragupta II show prosperity.

Education - Nalanda and learning. Nalanda in Bihar grew under the Guptas into the greatest monastic university of Asia: thousands of monks studied Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar and medicine in its halls and libraries; admission was by oral test at its gate, and students came from China, Korea, Tibet and Central Asia. Gupta education also flourished in Sanskrit centres like Ujjain and Pataliputra, with the gurukula tradition continuing; the era's cultivated ideal was the learned courtier-poet. Kumaragupta I is traditionally linked with Nalanda's early monastic growth.

Science - Aryabhatta. Aryabhatta (b. 476 CE) wrote the Aryabhatiya at 23: he gave the value of pi (3.1416), worked with the place-value decimal system and zero's place in notation, explained eclipses as shadows (not the demons of myth), and taught that the earth rotates on its axis causing the apparent motion of the stars. His astronomy (with Varahamihira's later synthesis) and mathematics, transmitted westward through the Arabs, gave the world the numerals we still call 'Arabic' but which India invented.

Medicine - the Sushrutha tradition. Indian medicine's classical surgical text, the Sushruta Samhita - teaching dissection, plastic surgery of the nose (rhinoplasty), lithotomy, cataract procedures, and the use of anaesthetics like wine and herbs - stands behind the era's fame in medicine; the Charaka Samhita (internal medicine) completed the canon. Gupta-period hospitals and charity houses (Fa-hien's account) show medical care organised for the public; physicians (vaidyas) were a recognised court profession.

Culture - Kalidasa and the Deogarh temple. Kalidasa, the greatest of the Navaratnas, perfected Sanskrit poetry and drama: Abhijnanashakuntalam (drama), Meghaduta (lyric), Raghuvamsha and Kumarasambhava (epics) - his nature-imagery and human tenderness set the classical style. In architecture, the Gupta age built the first structural stone temples: the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (UP) with its plinth, sanctum and shikhara, and carved panels of Vishnu, marks the transition from rock-cut to structural temples; Ajanta's murals (some Gupta-period) and Bhitari/Sarnath sculpture show the same classical grace. Puranic Hinduism - temple worship of Vishnu and Shiva with the avatar doctrine - flowered alongside Buddhism.

blocks.text: Fa-hien vs Harishena: Foreign pilgrim's eye-witness account of society versus court poet's eulogistic political record.
Samudragupta vs Chandragupta II: The conqueror of the Allahabad Pillar versus the empire-builder of Ujjain and patron of Kalidasa.
Bhukti vs Vishaya: Province under an uparika versus district under a vishayapati in the Gupta hierarchy.
Aryabhatiya vs Sushruta Samhita: Gupta-era astronomical-mathematical treatise versus the classical surgical text of Indian medicine.

questions.explanation: His Aryabhatiya (c. 499 CE) advanced maths and astronomy.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing him up with Sushruta or Kalidasa.

questions.prompt: Which Gupta ruler is called the 'Indian Napoleon'?
questions.answer: Samudragupta - for his sweeping conquests eulogised by Harishena.
questions.explanation: The title was coined by historian V.A. Smith.

questions.prompt: Name the two fields for which Nalanda was famous.
questions.answer: Buddhist philosophy and learning (also logic, grammar and medicine) - it was a great monastic university.
questions.explanation: Students came from all over Asia.
questions.commonMistake: Calling it a fortress or palace.

questions.prompt: What does Fa-hien's account tell us about Gupta society?
questions.answer: He describes prosperity and honest, happy people; mild punishments (fines rather than mutilation for most offences); vegetarianism widespread; Pataliputra's palace and charitable institutions, including free hospitals; the safety of travel for pilgrims. As a foreigner, his account confirms the inscriptions' picture of order and benevolence.
questions.commonMistake: Quoting him on conquests - he was not a chronicler of wars.

questions.prompt: State any two Gupta contributions to science.
questions.answer: Any two of: Aryabhatta's value of pi, place-value notation and the earth's rotation explanation; Varahamihira's encyclopaedic Brihatsamhita (astronomy-botany); metallurgy - the rust-free Iron Pillar of Mehrauli; medical advances continuing the Sushruta-Charaka tradition.
questions.commonMistake: Vague claims without names or works.

questions.prompt: What was the contribution of Sushrutha to medicine?
questions.answer: The Sushruta Samhita, the classical surgical text, teaches dissection, plastic surgery of the nose (rhinoplasty), lithotomy, cataract operations, the use of herbal anaesthetics, and a code of medical ethics - the foundation of Indian surgery that the Gupta age honoured.
questions.explanation: Name the text and its surgical content.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between Fa-hien's account and the Allahabad Pillar Inscription as sources.
questions.answer: Fa-hien's Record of Buddhist Kingdoms is a foreign pilgrim's eyewitness account of society and administration under Chandragupta II - descriptive, non-courtly, valuable for everyday life, religion and benevolence. The Allahabad Pillar Inscription (Prayaga Prashasti) is a court poet's (Harishena's) Sanskrit eulogy of Samudragupta - political, panegyric and detailed on conquests, but silent on common life. One shows the state from below/outside; the other from the throne; historians cross-check them with coins.
questions.explanation: Author, purpose, subject and reliability angles.
questions.commonMistake: Saying both are equally reliable on politics.

questions.prompt: Arrange in chronological order: Skandagupta, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II.
questions.answer: Chandragupta I (319-335 CE) -> Samudragupta (335-375 CE) -> Chandragupta II (375-413/15 CE) -> ... -> Skandagupta (455-467 CE).

questions.prompt: 'The Gupta Age was a golden age of culture.' Justify this statement with reference to education, science and literature.
questions.answer: Education: Nalanda grew into Asia's greatest monastic university - thousands of monks studying Buddhist philosophy, logic, grammar and medicine; admission by gate-test; students from China, Korea and Central Asia; Sanskrit learning flourished at Ujjain and Pataliputra. Science: Aryabhatta (b. 476 CE) gave pi's value, place-value notation, and explained eclipses and the earth's rotation; Varahamihira summarised astronomy and botany; the Iron Pillar of Mehrauli shows metallurgical mastery; the Sushruta-Charaka medical tradition was cultivated, with hospitals noted by Fa-hien. Literature and art: Kalidasa - the greatest Sanskrit poet-dramatist - wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta and Raghuvamsha; the Puranas took shape; the Deogarh Dashavatara temple marks the first structural stone temples; Ajanta's murals and Sarnath's Buddha sculpture perfected classical style. This concentration of achievement across fields, sustained by political stability and patronage, justifies the 'golden age' label - though historians add that the label coexisted with social inequality and the later feudal drift.
questions.explanation: Three heads with named evidence + a balanced conclusion.

questions.prompt: Give reasons: land grants (agrahara) both spread learning and weakened Gupta authority.
questions.answer: Grants of tax-free land to Brahmanas, temples and monasteries financed schools, libraries and new settlements in wilder areas - spreading agriculture and education. But the donated land, with its cultivators and sometimes administrative rights, passed permanently out of central control; recipients became landed intermediaries with local power, and state revenue shrank. Over generations this feudalising tendency sapped the Guptas' capacity to pay armies and officials - one cause of their decline.
questions.explanation: Both sides of the effect must be shown.
